summary: A 1920s pole lookout on Mt. Hood was rebuilt twice after snow damage, and the 1957 R-6 tower that resulted is now a year-round Forest Service rental.

access.note: Drive-up access in summer; winter access is up to 3 miles by ski/snowshoe/snowmobile from Billy Bob Sno-Park, requiring a Northwest Forest Pass.

visit.trail_note: Available year-round as a Forest Service rental; no drinking water on site.

events.note: First lookout: a small cab on a pole tower, established in the 1920s.
L-4 cab erected on a 30-foot pole tower.
The 1932 tower collapsed under heavy snow.
Present 30-foot treated-timber tower with R-6 flat cab built.
Listed on the National Historic Lookout Register September 4, 2011.

evidence.quote: The first Five Mile Butte Lookout on the Mt. Hood National Forest was a pole tower in the 1920s. In 1932 an L-4 cab atop a 30' pole tower was erected, but it collapsed under snow ten years later, to be replaced again with another L-4 on a stronger tower. This R-6 cab on a 30' tower was built in 1957 and is in the rental program.
The present 30' treated timber tower topped with an R-6 flat cab was built in 1957. The lookout is presently on the Recreation Rental program.

evidence.supports: 1920s pole cab, 1932 standard tower, 1942 destruction, 1957 rebuild
evidence.quote: The lookout was originally a small cab on a 30-foot tower, established in the 1920s. In 1932, a standard lookout tower was built to replace the earlier lookout, but was destroyed by heavy snow in 1942. A non-typical lookout structure was rebuilt at the site in 1957.
The tower sits on Fivemile Butte, at an elevation of 4,627 feet. It is surrounded by ponderosa pine, Douglas fir and western hemlock forests.

evidence.supports: year-round rental and winter access route
evidence.quote: Fivemile Butte Lookout is available for reservation year-round. ... During winter driving conditions, from early fall to late spring, the lookout can only be accessed by skiing, snowmobiling or snowshoeing up to 3 miles one way from a parking area at the Billy Bob Sno-Park.
Drinking water is not available at the tower
A variety of wildlife, including wild turkeys, grouse and blue jays, as well as deer, elk, coyotes, cougars and bears, frequent the area.

evidence.supports: Northwest Forest Pass requirement, Barlow and Hood River Ranger Districts
evidence.quote: A Northwest Forest Pass is required for the parking area at Billy Bob Sno-park... For current conditions, please call Barlow Ranger District office at 541-467-2291 or the Hood River Ranger District office at 541-352-6002.

notes_for_editor: No current staffing status found in sources, so staffing left as unknown rather than guessed; the brief's 1957 built-year is confirmed by all three sources.
